evaluation.positioning_hook: A lonely young woman turns a shy library flirtation into a full-blown obsession, stalking the man she thinks is hers until desire curdles into captivity and cannibalistic possession.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediate and genre-legible, but the audience is narrower than a broad commercial thriller because the material escalates into extreme psychosexual horror. The premise has clear cult appeal and strong late-night/genre-festival value, but it is not built for four-quadrant reach.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The central engine is easy to explain: a first-date crush becomes stalking, then captivity, then bodily horror. The script announces its premise early and keeps returning to the same obsessional spine, even if the scene-by-scene execution is loose.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Allison is the clear engine and has a vivid, escalating fixation that gives the role bite, while Dante reads as a grounded counterweight with enough warmth to make the danger land. The supporting cast is thin, though, and the character ecosystem is built more for the central pairing than for a broader ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The praying-mantis metaphor, the eroticized stalking, and the final cannibalistic payoff give the script a distinctive, nasty identity. It is still working inside familiar obsession-horror territory, but the specific animal logic and fetishized intimacy make it feel authored.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The relationship escalates in a clear line from library meet-cute to invasive fixation to violent possession, which keeps the engine moving. The middle section repeats variations on texting, calling, and hanging out, so the momentum is more cumulative than propulsive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script lands on a fresh, instantly readable twist: romantic yearning expressed as predatory consumption. The praying mantis motif and the final shed sequence make the concept memorable, even if the emotional logic is more visceral than nuanced.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is mostly a contemporary dating-and-home setting with a few repeated locations: library, diner, car, house, room, shed. There is some texture in the construction job, the school references, and the social-media stalking, but the world functions as a container for the obsession rather than a story-generating system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific register: awkward teen/young-adult flirtation sliding into erotic dread and body horror. The tonal identity is unusual because it keeps the language casual and almost cute while the behavior becomes increasingly grotesque.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper psychology in Allison’s identity erosion, her imitation of Dante’s ex, and the praying-mantis poetry, but the script mostly externalizes the obsession rather than layering it. The surface experience is strong; the deeper interior life is suggested more than dramatized.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is fundamentally a two-character engine, and even that engine is asymmetrical because Allison dominates the story’s psychological drive. The supporting players function as functional markers rather than recurring relationship nodes with their own story energy.

lead_characters.name: Allison
lead_characters.demographics: young woman, late teens to early 20s, socially isolated, contemporary setting
lead_characters.hook: Allison starts as a shy, bookish girl with a soft-spoken flirtation style and quickly reveals a terrifying capacity for fixation, mimicry, and escalation. She is lonely enough to romanticize attention, unstable enough to turn affection into surveillance, and physically expressive in a way that makes her obsession feel both intimate and dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory in the vein of Mia Goth in Pearl or Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl — a role that lets an actor pivot from vulnerable awkwardness to unhinged control. The prize is the full-body transformation: flirtation, humiliation, erotic compulsion, breakdown, and monstrous commitment.

lead_characters.name: Dante
lead_characters.demographics: young man, late teens to early 20s, working-class, contemporary setting
lead_characters.hook: Dante is the approachable, slightly awkward guy whose warmth and normalcy make him easy to trust and easy to target. He has enough personality to feel like a real person — playful, patient, a little self-conscious — but the script uses him primarily as the object of Allison’s fixation and the emotional baseline for the horror.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded, likable counterpoint in a horror lead pair, similar to the boyfriend roles in Fresh or Barbarian. The showcase is in playing charm under pressure, then fear, then violated helplessness without losing humanity.

lead_characters.name: Librarian
lead_characters.hook: A brief but functional presence who helps anchor the opening meet-cute and gives the library scene a lived-in everyday texture. She exists as a social witness to the first exchange and the note-in-the-book reveal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small character-actor beat with one clean scene of observational realism, the kind of role that can land if cast with a sharp comic or grounded indie performer.

lead_characters.name: Waitress
lead_characters.hook: The waitress is a practical scene partner who gives the diner sequence motion, lightly comments on the couple’s chemistry, and helps the date feel public and ordinary before the story turns private and predatory.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact service-role part with a little comic timing and social texture, the kind of scene that can pop if played with naturalism.

lead_characters.name: Andrea
lead_characters.demographics: young woman, late teens to early 20s, ex-girlfriend
lead_characters.hook: Andrea is mostly an off-screen pressure point, but she matters because Allison studies her as a template and a rival. She becomes part of the script’s jealousy architecture and helps define the obsessive logic of replacement.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a brief but useful off-screen-to-on-screen presence for an actor in a flashback or confrontation beat, with the kind of relational specificity that can make a small role memorable.

lead_characters.name: Ex
lead_characters.demographics: young woman, late teens to early 20s
lead_characters.hook: A confrontational former girlfriend whose presence is mostly mediated through phone calls, social media, and flashback fragments. She functions as a warning sign and a source of comparison for Allison’s imitation behavior.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but sharp dramatic beat role with one confrontational scene and a clear emotional function.

lead_characters.name: Driver
lead_characters.hook: A cab driver with a brief, functional exchange that underscores Allison’s isolation and the aftermath of the breakup. The role is minimal but gives the ending a mundane, chilling normalcy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a tiny character role, useful for a grounded performer who can make a few lines feel real.

casting_characteristics: supporting roles are brief and age-flexible

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: mostly interior with some exterior car, park, and street scenes

technical.vfx_details: No major VFX; practical blood, gore, and body-horror makeup for the final captivity and cannibalism sequence.
technical.sfx_needs: practical blood effects, gore prosthetics, broken-glass injury, handcuff/captivity setup

rights_flags.detail: social media platforms and maps are referenced generically, but no single brand is central enough to flag as clearance-critical

platform_fit.recommended_lane: streaming or premium cable genre feature
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to genre streaming, specialty theatrical, or premium-cable-style distribution

budget.note: Contemporary, mostly contained interiors and a small number of practical gore setups keep the spend controlled. The final shed sequence needs strong makeup and blood effects, but there is no heavy VFX or large-scale action.

casting.note: Allison is a demanding lead because the role has to move from awkward charm to erotic fixation to full psychosis without losing audience attention. Dante also needs enough warmth and naturalism to make the turn from romance to horror land.

development.note: The script’s scene-to-scene momentum depends on the obsession escalating cleanly from meet-cute to stalking to captivity, and the middle section repeats several texting/date beats. The concept is clear, but the execution will be judged on whether each escalation feels inevitable rather than episodic.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre fans who like intimate, female-driven horror with a strong performance centerpiece and a nasty final turn.
audience_target.demographics: 18-34 skew, slightly female-leaning, horror-native audience, streamer-first viewers, festival/indie genre crowd

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, a small cast, and practical gore effects keep this in indie-feature territory.

types_of_buyers: producer-directors looking for a performance-led horror vehicle
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the intimate, performance-forward horror lane where a strong lead can carry the marketing. The body-horror ending and obsessive romance angle make it attractive to buyers who want something nasty but still character-led.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with no clear franchise or spinoff vector beyond the central Allison-Dante story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The obsession engine is instantly legible.
strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which is a real advantage in genre packaging and streamer browsing. That clarity helps this play as a fast-read, easy-pitch horror feature for executives and audiences who want the hook immediately.
strengths.evidence: The library meet-cute turns into stalking, social-media surveillance, imitation of the ex, and finally captivity in the shed.

strengths.what_it_means: The script gives an actress a full descent role with flirtation, shame, erotic fixation, breakdown, and predatory control. That is exactly the kind of part that can attract a strong indie or horror-facing performer looking for a calling-card turn.
strengths.evidence: Her shift from nervous phone calls to copying Dante’s ex to the final cannibalistic possession sequence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The praying-mantis motif gives the script a brandable identity.
strengths.what_it_means: The animal metaphor turns the obsession into a memorable visual and thematic signature, which helps the film stand out in a crowded horror market. It also gives marketing a clean symbolic hook without needing to over-explain the plot.
strengths.evidence: Allison’s poem about being a praying mantis and the final image of her with Dante’s heart.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tonal contrast is commercially useful.
strengths.what_it_means: The script keeps the dialogue casual and almost cute while the behavior becomes increasingly disturbing, which creates a strong unease curve. That contrast is attractive to buyers looking for elevated genre that can play both as relationship drama and horror.
strengths.evidence: The diner flirtation, the awkward texting, and the later invasive surveillance all live in the same conversational register.

strengths.what_it_means: The movie can be made without large-scale action, major VFX, or a sprawling cast, which makes it easier to finance and package. That opens the door to first-time feature directors and indie financiers who want a controlled spend with a strong genre payoff.
strengths.evidence: Most scenes live in the library, diner, car, house, bedroom, and shed, with practical gore driving the climax.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept indie horror package: one standout female lead role, a simple obsession engine, and a contained production footprint. The praying-mantis metaphor and body-horror finale give it a memorable identity that can travel in the elevated-genre lane without needing a large cast or expensive set pieces.

items.area: The middle section repeats the same beat.
items.detail: Several scenes cycle through texting, awkward calls, and low-stakes dates before the obsession fully mutates into danger. That makes the script feel more cumulative than propulsive in the middle, which is the main pacing conversation a buyer will have.

items.area: Allison’s psychology is more external than layered.
items.detail: We see the behavior clearly — stalking, imitation, jealousy, possession — but the script gives limited interior complexity beyond the obsession itself. That keeps the role vivid, but it also narrows the emotional range of the movie to one dominant note.

items.area: The final gore turn is a buyer filter.
items.detail: The shed sequence goes all the way into explicit cannibalistic body horror, which sharply narrows the audience and the buyer pool. For some genre buyers that is the point; for others it pushes the material from elevated thriller into hard-sell niche horror.

items.area: The supporting cast is thin by design.
items.detail: Outside Allison and Dante, most characters are functional scene devices rather than durable relationship engines. That is fine for a contained feature, but it limits the script’s broader social texture and leaves the movie heavily dependent on the lead performance.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the premise — it is the repetition inside the obsession arc and the fact that the movie lives or dies on Allison’s performance. The explicit final body-horror turn is memorable, but it also narrows the buyer pool to genre-specific players comfortable with extreme material.
